ep28.title: The Barcode Reportedly Started In The Sand
ep28.desc:
Every day a red beam sweeps across a pattern of black lines and a register beeps. By its inventor's own account, that pattern began as lines drawn with four fingers in the sand on a beach in Florida. The first design was a circle, and the circle lost. This is the story of the barcode, and of two inventors, one of whom never saw it work in a shop.

Chapters
0:00 Intro
0:30 Lines In The Sand
2:22 Twenty Years Too Early
4:09 The Rectangle Wins
5:54 A Pack Of Gum
7:26 So, who invented it?
8:10 Sources

A note on the evidence: the beach story is Joseph Woodland's own account, and sources differ on the exact date (winter 1948 to 1949). The executive who asked the dean for a checkout reader is not named because the name rests on a single source. The sale of the patent (reportedly for $15,000, to Philco, with the rights later passing to RCA) is reported without a year because sources conflict. The committee's choice of the rectangular code is given as "spring 1973" because sources differ by a few days. The pack size, the price (67 cents) and the reason gum was chosen for the first scan in 1974 are reported differently by different sources; the film says so. The pack of gum itself is not in the Smithsonian; one early scanner is.

- NPR and WFAE reports; George Laurer's own memoir of the UPC; Engineering and Technology History Wiki
- Business Week (1976); NBER working paper on scanner adoption; Supermarket News; Indiana Encyclopedia (Marsh Supermarkets)
- Wikipedia (supporting only)

Footage disclosure
Real archival footage is about 52 percent of the running time; the rest is original hand-drawn explainer animation by Odd Making (about 228 s, 46 percent) plus the sources card. There is no real footage of the 1948 sand drawing, of Silver, Woodland or Laurer, or of the first scan in 1974; none was found in public-domain collections. Archival footage is period illustration only and much of it is older than the sentence it sits under: the supermarket and computer footage is from 1960 and is used as a stand-in for the 1970s (it is labelled with its true year on screen). Black and white films were sepia-graded; all were cropped. Source credits appear on screen.
